back: protecting the two top threat vectors attackers use, email and the web, because they are the most popular protocols for individuals and organizations.
the company Cisco acquired that created the products now called Cisco Secure Web Appliance and Cisco Secure Email.
web proxy, threat analytics engine, antimalware engine, policy management, and reporting in one physical or virtual appliance. Formerly called the Web Security Appliance (WSA).
email gateway that handles all SMTP connections for an organization. Formerly called the Email Security Appliance (ESA).

centralizes management and reporting for multiple Cisco Secure Email and Cisco Secure Web Appliance devices. Cisco has since renamed it Cisco Secure Email and Web Manager; that name is not in the book but is worth knowing.
the operating system of Cisco Secure Web Appliance, Cisco Secure Email, and Cisco SMA. Named for its optimized asynchronous handling of email and web transactions.
Cisco threat intelligence group whose feeds the content security products digest.
analyzes and categorizes unknown URLs and blocks sites that fall below a defined security policy or threshold. Looks at more than 200 factors and gives a score from minus 10 to plus 10.
combines traditional URL filtering with real-time dynamic content analysis. Allows granular acceptable use policy (AUP) creation and warns users about quota and bandwidth conditions.
inspects or blocks applications that policy does not allow, including micro-applications inside allowed sites, like Facebook games.
detects and stops hidden threats in cloud apps by using AVC plus integration with a CASB.
cloud app security service, such as Cisco Cloudlock.
supports McAfee, Sophos, and Webroot engines.
based on Cisco Talos intelligence, updated every three to five minutes.
stops sensitive data from leaving the network, maliciously or by accident.
runs an unknown file in a sandbox to watch its behavior, through Cisco Secure Endpoint and Cisco Secure Malware Analytics, which use machine learning to set the threat level.
keeps re-examining downloaded files over an extended period of time.
the verdict on a file, such as Unknown, Clean, or Malware.
a file disposition that has changed after the fact.
anomaly detection on HTTP and HTTPS traffic, tuned by new threat information from the system and Talos. Can find confirmed threats even when HTTPS inspection is disabled.
Cisco sandbox, formerly Cisco AMP Threat Grid. Available as a cloud service or an on-premises appliance.
sits between HTTP clients (web browsers, or APIs in machine-to-machine traffic) and HTTP servers. Uses two sets of TCP sockets per request: client to proxy, and proxy to web server.
the client is configured to use the proxy and sends all web traffic to it.
clients don't know a proxy exists. Network devices redirect web traffic to it.
a file that tells browsers which proxy settings to use.
advertises PAC settings to clients, using the auto-detect proxy settings in every modern browser.
Microsoft tool that can push and lock browser proxy settings.
the client negotiates a proxy connection with SOCKS protocol messages, then talks to the appliance over SOCKS.
Cisco-developed content-routing protocol that redirects traffic flows in real time. Has built-in load balancing, scaling, fault tolerance, and service-assurance (failsafe) mechanisms.
a set of devices providing or using the same redirection service. Named by a predefined keyword such as web-cache, or by a dynamic service ID number such as 10 or 20.
routes matched traffic to a chosen next hop, here the web appliance.
a switch or router that redirects traffic based on Layer 4 ports.
the place in the network where a redirection device sends traffic to a transparent proxy.
in Cisco Firewall Management Center (FMC), an ordered container of FlexConfig objects used to configure features FMC does not directly support.
Apache Velocity scripting commands, Cisco ASA commands, and variables. Acts as a program that generates ASA commands to deploy to devices.
forwarded requests keep the client's source IP instead of the appliance's.
lightweight HTTP-like protocol that forwards web requests to external DLP servers or content scanners. Secure ICAP is the other choice offered.
certificate status checking, configurable in the HTTPS proxy.
identifies the user behind a web request, instead of only the IP address.
maps identification profiles and users to rules, including time-based restrictions.
controls HTTPS decryption once the HTTPS proxy is configured.
manages data uploads to the web.
blocks malware uploads.
an administrator-defined category for URL filtering.
authenticates users without a prompt, using the authentication state from another trusted source. Considered SSO; users don't know a proxy exists.
an AD or LDAP authentication server definition.
done through the web browser. Not transparent.
transparent authentication with AD domain credentials. Needs a compatible browser.
mainly for Windows clients. The more secure option.
how transactions are tied to a user after a successful login.
the protocol for email transactions on the Internet.
what most people call the mail server. Transfers email from sender to recipient. Also called a mail router, mail transport agent, or mail exchanger (MX).
part of an MTA that does final delivery to the mailbox.
the email client or reader on a computer or mobile device.
part of an MTA that accepts new messages from an MUA using SMTP.
client protocol that keeps messages on the server. The client shows them directly from the server, but can also download them for archiving.
application-layer protocol a client uses to retrieve (download) email from a remote server.

DNS resource record naming the mail server that accepts mail for a domain. A preference value sets priority when there are several. That the lowest value is tried first is not in the book but is worth knowing.
bulk mail such as newsletters that the user once agreed to receive. The definition is not in the book; the book only lists it as content a mail policy can target.
handles incoming SMTP connection requests and defines the email processing service on a Cisco Secure Email interface.
accepts email from the Internet.
accepts email from internal systems.
Ironport's sender reputation service. Score from minus 10 to plus 10.
on by default. Provide a dynamic quarantine, also called a DELAY quarantine.
the malware engine used for extra scans and file analysis.
defines which recipients a public listener accepts. Not to be confused with a remote-access Trojan.
a set of rules for suspect, sensitive, or malicious content you don't want entering or leaving the network.
where SPF and DKIM verification are configured.
lets recipients verify the sender's IP address against DNS TXT records listing a domain's authorized mail gateways.
gateway-based cryptographic signing of outgoing mail. Puts verification data in a header so recipients can check integrity. Publishes public keys in DNS TXT records. The book spells it "Domain Keys".
a DKIM-related specification.
data that identifies a person.
redirected by WCCP and PBR. By default the web appliance only redirects and decodes port 80 HTTP traffic.
matched in the WCCP and PBR ACLs. Decrypted only when the HTTPS proxy is enabled.
the examples match it with the ftp keyword. The number 21 is not in the book but is worth knowing.
the range matched with FTP in the redirect ACLs. The book doesn't explain what these ports are for.
the dig example queries the server at 192.168.88.1 port 53.
carries the WPAD URL as a string.
all Internet email transactions. TCP 25 is not in the book but is worth knowing; TCP 587 for submission is also not in the book but worth knowing.
the recipient's client gets mail from the internal server. IMAP TCP 143 (993 secure) and POP3 TCP 110 (995 secure) are not in the book but are worth knowing.
version 2 is used on the appliance. UDP 2048 is not in the book but is worth knowing.
to external DLP servers. TCP 1344 for ICAP is not in the book but is worth knowing.
the appliance's SOCKS proxy. TCP 1080 is the usual SOCKS port; not in the book but worth knowing.
the book gives none. The web appliance listens on 80 and 3128 by default, and 8080 is also common; not in the book but worth knowing.
the appliance can tunnel CONNECT requests on specific ports.

front: access-list HTTP-TRAFFIC permit tcp 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 any eq www
back: matches HTTP from 10.1.1.0/24. The same line for 10.1.2.0 covers the second subnet.

front: access-list HTTPS-TRAFFIC permit tcp 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 any eq https
back: matches HTTPS. Repeated for 10.1.2.0.

front: access-list FTP-TRAFFIC permit tcp 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 any eq ftp
back: matches FTP. Repeated for 10.1.2.0.

front: access-list FTP-TRAFFIC permit tcp 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 any range 11000 11006
back: matches the FTP port range. Repeated for 10.1.2.0.

front: access-list WSA extended permit ip host 10.1.2.3 any
back: identifies the web appliance at 10.1.2.3.

front: wccp web-cache redirect-list HTTP-TRAFFIC group-list WSA
back: the predefined web-cache service for HTTP, sent to the WSA group.
dynamic service 10 for FTP.
dynamic service 20 for HTTPS.

front: wccp interface inside web-cache redirect in, wccp interface inside 10 redirect in, wccp interface inside 20 redirect in
back: turn on redirection inbound on the inside (source) interface.
ACL with **permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www**, the same for 10.1.2.0, and **eq 443** lines for both subnets. Switches use wildcard masks.
ACL with **eq ftp** and **range 11000 11006** lines for both subnets. The book prints "10.1.1.00.0.0.255" with the space missing; it should read 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255.

front: ip access-list standard WSA with permit 10.1.3.3
back: where to send the traffic. Here the appliance is 10.1.3.3, not the 10.1.2.3 used in the ASA example.

front: ip wccp web-cache redirect-list HTTP-TRAFFIC group-list WSA, ip wccp 10 redirect-list FTP-TRAFFIC group-list WSA, ip wccp 20 redirect-list HTTPS-TRAFFIC group-list WSA
back: create the WCCP lists. The book is inconsistent here: these reference HTTP-TRAFFIC and HTTPS-TRAFFIC, but the switch example only created one ACL named WEB-TRAFFIC.

front: interface vlan88 with ip wccp web-cache redirect in, ip wccp 10 redirect in, ip wccp 20 redirect in
back: turn on redirection on the source interface.
